nuggets.title: APNs rate limit drops critical alerts

scenario.symptoms: During a security incident, password-reset pushes failed for 18% of users. APNs returned HTTP 429 and the service had no retry backoff or priority queue separation.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Marketing and transactional notifications share one worker pool and the same provider credentials. Bursty marketing traffic consumed the provider token bucket.

incident.headline: Shared provider queue lets marketing exhaust rate limits for transactional pushes

agenda.goal: Deliver critical notifications even when providers throttle bulk traffic.
agenda.opener: Password-reset pushes failed during a marketing blast—how would you isolate and protect transactional delivery?

evidence.strong: Separate queues/credentials per priority, exponential backoff on 429, circuit breakers, and shed lower-priority traffic under pressure.
evidence.adequate: Retries all sends equally without priority.
evidence.weak: Single worker pool for all notification types.

misconceptions.challenge: What happens to provider limits if every worker hammers retries?

probes: How do you prove transactional SLA during a campaign?
Should marketing and security share APNs topic credentials?
hints: Priority queues are common for SMS/push providers.
Backoff headers from providers are a signal.
agenda.referenceFix: Split transactional and bulk into isolated dispatchers with reserved throughput, honor Retry-After, pause marketing when transactional backlog grows, and alert on 429 rates.

scenario.symptoms: Users received the same promo push twice within 30 seconds. Logs show two delivery attempts with identical payload hash but different worker attempt IDs.
scenario.interviewerSetup: The outbound queue is at-least-once. Workers crash after sending to APNs but before marking the job complete, causing redelivery without idempotency keys.

incident.headline: Worker crash after send causes duplicate delivery on queue redelivery

agenda.opener: Same push arrived twice—where should idempotency live in this pipeline?

evidence.strong: Idempotency key per user+template+event, dedupe store with TTL, provider collapse-id, and ack-after-durable log.
evidence.adequate: Dedupes only at enqueue time, not after provider send.

probes: When do you write the dedupe record relative to the APNs call?
How long must dedupe keys live?
hints: APNs supports collapse identifiers for duplicates.
agenda.referenceFix: Check dedupe store before send, record send intent atomically, use provider collapse-id, and mark queue jobs complete only after durable delivery log write.

nuggets.title: App silently drops notifications over quota

scenario.symptoms: Enterprise customers report missing in-app alerts while push volume looked normal. Internal metrics show 35% of enqueue requests rejected with HTTP 429 from the quota middleware.
scenario.interviewerSetup: Per-tenant quotas are enforced at enqueue time with a hard fail and no visibility to product teams. Burst traffic from webhooks exhausts shared tenant buckets.

incident.headline: Hard quota rejections silently discard notifications without tenant visibility

agenda.goal: Enforce fair quotas while giving tenants predictable behavior under bursts.
agenda.opener: Alerts vanished for a tenant hitting quota—how should quotas work without silent data loss?

evidence.strong: Token bucket with burst allowance, priority tiers, structured 429 with retry-after, metrics/alerts per tenant, and optional paid overage queue.
evidence.adequate: Fixed cap with hard fail but adds logging only.
evidence.weak: Unbounded enqueue leading to provider bans.

probes: Should transactional alerts bypass marketing quotas?
How does the client backoff when quota is exceeded?
hints: Silent drops are worse than delayed delivery.
Expose quota usage in tenant APIs.
agenda.referenceFix: Use token buckets with burst, separate transactional vs bulk quotas, return explicit retry-after, surface usage metrics to tenants, and optionally queue overflow instead of dropping.
